abstract.p: The present invention discloses a method for classifying a library of chemical compounds and generating new chemical compounds to improve the diversity of the library. More particularly, the present invention creates an extended ring structure classification system, assigns chemical compounds from a library to categories within the classification system, recognizes empty categories, and generates new chemical structures to fill the empty categories in order to improve the range of structures represented by the library.

L'invention concerne un procédé pour établir la classification d'une bibliothèque de composés chimiques et pour générer de nouveaux composés chimiques afin de diversifier cette bibliothèque. L'invention permet notamment de créer un système de classification à structure en cercle élargi, de classer les composés chimiques compris dans la bibliothèque selon certaines catégories, de reconnaître les catégories vides et de générer de nouvelles structures chimiques pour remplir les catégories vides de manière à améliorer la variété des structures représentées dans cette bibliothèque.

description.p: A SYSTEM FOR THE CLASSIFICATION AND GENERATION OF
CHEMICAL COMPOUNDS
RELATED APPLICATIONS
This is a continuation-in-part of U.S. application no. 09/019,175, filed February 5, 1998.
FIELD OF THE INVENTION

The present invention relates generally to a method for classifying a library of chemical compounds and for generating new chemical structures. More particularly, the present invention creates a ring structure classification system, assigns chemical compounds from a library to categories within the classification system, recognizes empty categories, and generates new chemical structures to fill the empty categories in order to improve the range of structures represented by the library.
BACKGROUND

Conventional methods for creating chemical compounds with desired properties and activities identify lead compounds, create variants of the lead compounds and evaluate the variant compounds with respect to the desired properties and activities. Conventional methods search existing chemical compound libraries and utilize a combination of empirical science and chemical intuition to identify lead compounds.

Conventional methods for creating chemical compounds have a fundamental limitation because of their dependency on existing chemical compound libraries for the identification of
lead compounds. First, the chemical library may not have compounds with a wide range of different structures. Second the chemical library may contain many compounds with a similar structure which increases the difficulty associated with managing the information in the chemical libraries to identify lead compounds. Accordingly, the utility of the conventional methods for creating chemical compounds is limited by the amount of diversity in the existing chemical libraries.

Conventional methods for creating chemical compounds have a further disadvantage because of their dependency on chemical intuition to identify lead compounds from existing chemical compound libraries. The Chemical Abstracts registry file exceeds fifteen million compounds. The large number of chemical compounds limits the utility of methods which rely on an individual's chemical intuition to screen the chemical compound libraries by manually processing a large amount of unorganized data to identify lead compounds. "Chemical intuition, at least to date, has not proven to be a particularly good source of lead compounds for the drug discovery process". See Rudy M. Baum, "Combinatorial Approaches Provide Fresh Leads for Medicinal Chemistry", (C&EN, Feb. 7, 1994, pp. 20-26) .

Research in combinatorial chemistry has attempted to address some of the limitations associated with the conventional methods for creating chemical compounds. Typical approaches in combinatorial chemistry form a library of chemical compounds by combining a set of chemical building blocks in every possible way for a given compound length.

However, the enormous number of possible combinations limits the feasibility of these approaches.
U.S. Patent 5,463,564 ("the '564 Patent") discloses an enhanced combinatorial chemistry system which selectively combines chemical building blocks in accordance with desired physical, chemical, and bioactive properties instead of generating every possible combination. Specifically, the '564 patent discloses a chemical synthesis system to create a directed diversity chemical library by selectively combining a number of building blocks such as reagents in accordance with robotic synthesis instructions which are determined from the desired physical, chemical, and bioactive properties. After . . . . creating an initial chemical library, the system analyzes the compounds in the directed diversity library, constructs structure-activity and structure-property models and generates new robotic synthesis instructions, and generates a modified directed diversity chemical library. This system repeats this procedure in an iterative fashion until the properties of the chemical compounds in the library match the desired properties .

Additional research has disclosed techniques to analyze existing libraries of chemical compounds. One exemplary system uses shape description methods to analyze a database of commercially available drugs and to prepare a list of common drug shapes. See Guy . Bemis and Mark A. Murcko, J., "The
Properties of Known Drugs. 1. Molecular Frameworks", Med.

Chem. 1996, 39, 2887-2893. This system uses a molecular framework hierarchical description comprising ring systems, linkers and side chain atoms to classify molecules. The system has a number of uses. First, drug discovery methods can use this classification scheme to identify well represented frameworks . Next , combinatorial chemistry methods can use the linkers and ring systems identified by this classification scheme in the automated generation of chemical compound libraries. Finally, this classification scheme
evaluates particular libraries of chemical compounds by comparing the molecular frameworks of the chemical compounds to the molecular frameworks of known drugs .

c While previous research in combinatorial chemistry and the analysis of chemical libraries have made improvements over conventional methods for the creation of chemical compounds, there remains a need for a system which efficiently classifies chemical compounds from a library according to their structure, identifies the structures of the chemical compounds 0 . . which are missing from the library, and generates the missing chemical structures in order to improve the range of structures represented by the library.
SUMMARY OF THE INVENTION

In general, it is an object of the present invention to provide a classification system to efficiently classify the chemical compounds in a library and to subsequently identify the structures which are missing from the library. 0
It is a further general object of the present invention to generate the missing chemical structures to improve the range of structures represented by the library.

It is a object of the present invention to achieve the general objectives by defining a method for classifying a molecule having a plurality of atoms, bonds and rings comprising the steps of : constructing a graph representation for the molecule comprising a plurality of vertices and edges corresponding to the plurality of atoms and bonds of the molecule, said graph representation having a plurality of simple cycles corresponding to the plurality of rings of the molecule,-
determining the lengths of a designated number of the longest of said plurality of simple cycles in said graph representation; and representing said longest simple cycles with a table of entries, each of said entries having a first field and a corresponding second field wherein said first field contains said longest simple cycle lengths and said second field contains the number of said simple cycles having said corresponding longest simple cycle length.

It is also an object of the present invention to achieve the general objectives by defining a method for achieving diversity in a library of molecules comprising the steps of: assigning each molecule in the library to one of a plurality of entries using the method of claim 1; and generating a plurality of new chemical structures to fill empty ones of said plurality of entries.

It is a further object of the present invention to achieve the general objectives by further defining the method for achieving diversity in a library of molecules wherein the method further comprising the steps of : identifying isomorphic chemical structures in said plurality of entries; and removing said isomorphic chemical structures.

It is a further object of the present invention to achieve the general objectives by further defining the method for achieving diversity in a library of molecules wherein the method further comprising the steps of: identifying unrealistic chemical structures in said plurality of entries; and
removing said unrealistic chemical structures.

DETAILED DESCRIPTION OF THE PREFERRED EMBODIMENT

Fig. 1 provides an overview of the classification method of the present invention. In step 100, the method defines a classification system. This classification system comprises a plurality of categories. In step 110, the method inputs a library of molecules and classifies the library of molecules. To classify the library of molecules, step 120 assigns each molecule in the library to a category in the classification system. Step 120 outputs a completed classification system. The completed classification system identifies the molecules which were assigned to each category of the system. Step 120 inputs the completed classification system and identifies the structures of the molecules which are missing from the library of molecules. Step 120 identifies the structures of the absent molecules by locating empty categories m the completed classification system. Step 120 outputs a list of empty categories .
The classification system identifies each of its categories by a sequence of non-negative integers having a designated length. The first integer in the sequence c represents the length of the longest ring in the molecule. Each successive integer in the sequence represents the length of successively shorter constituent rings in the molecule.
Fig. 2 provides a partial illustration of an exemplary classification system 200. The exemplary classification 0 system 200 has a longest possible ring length of twenty-seven.

The sequence of non-negative integers of the exemplary classification system 200 has a designated length of two. The sequence of non-negative integers, "27, 26" identifies the first category 210 of the exemplary 5 classification system 200. Accordingly, the first category 210 will contain molecules having a longest ring length of 27 and a next longest ring length of 26. Similarly, the second category 220 of the exemplary classification system 200 will contain molecules having a longest ring length of 27 and a o next longest ring length of 25. Likewise, the final category
230 shown in the exemplary classification system 200 will contain molecules having a longest ring length of 3 and a next longest ring length of 0. In other words, the final category
230 will contain molecules having only rings with a length of

In the preferred embodiment, the designated length of the sequence of non-negative integers of the classification system ranges from three to seven and the maximum possible ring length supported by the classification system is about twenty- 0 seven. In a series of alternate embodiments, the designated length of the sequence of non-negative integers of the classification system ranges from one to twenty-five.
Further, as indicated in the discussion below, the classification system has features which enable support for larger maximum possible ring lengths.

Fig. 3 displays the number of categories in the classification system as a function of the designated length of the sequence of non-negative integers. For example, the classification system will have twenty-five categories with a designated length of the sequence of non-negative integers of one. Similarly, the classification system will have fifteen . . . thousand, two hundred seventy five categories with a designated length of the sequence of non-negative integers of four.

The designated length of the sequence of non-negative integers determines the resolution of the classification system. Specifically, the categories of a classification system having a smaller designated length of the sequence of non-negative integers will hold more molecules than the categories of a classification system having a larger designated sequence length. Accordingly, the resolution of the classification system can be adjusted by changing the designated length of the sequence of non-negative integers.

Fig. 4 and Fig. 5 illustrate the utility and context of the classification system of the present invention. Fig. 4 shows the relationship between small molecules 420-495 and large molecules or receptors 410. Chemical compound libraries hold small molecules 420 - 495. To have utility, a small molecule (420 - 495) must be compatible with a large molecule or receptor 410. As shown in Fig 4., the small molecule 490 is compatible with the large molecule 410. A chemical compound library should contain compounds with a wide range of structures to increase the probability that a member of the
chemical compound library will be compatible with a large molecule or receptor 410. In other words, a chemical compound library should contain molecules having a diverse range of structures .

It is useful to measure diversity with molecular structure because molecules with different structures will be compatible with different large molecules or receptors. Accordingly, the classification system measures diversity among the chemical compounds in a library in a useful manner . . . . because it distinguishes molecules according to their structure .

The classification system of the present invention achieves a chemical compound library having a diverse set of structures within the context shown in Fig. 5. A large number of academic research groups labeled as makers 510 synthesize very large numbers of molecules. For example, the Chemical Abstracts registry file presently contains over fifteen million compounds. The pharmaceutical and agrochemical industry labeled as users 530 search the very large numbers of molecules to find molecules with biological activity. The classification system of the present invention is used by the intermediary 520 to create a library of chemical compounds having a diverse set of structures from the very large number of chemical compounds supplied by the makers 510 to ease the task performed by the users 530.

The intermediary 520 uses the present invention to assign the molecules in the library of chemical compounds to the categories of the classification system. The intermediary 520 identifies the structures of the molecules which are missing from the library of chemical compounds by identifying empty or sparsely populated categories in the classification system.
Using this information, the intermediary 520 can add molecules with the identified structures to the library by collecting them from the makers 510.

Similarly, the intermediary 520 identifies the structures of the molecules which are overly represented in the library of chemical compounds. Using this information, the intermediary 520 can remove compounds with the identified structure to address the difficulty associated with managing information experienced by the users 530. By limiting the . . . . . number of molecules m the library having a similar structure, the intermediary can also reduce the cost of the library to the users 530 while providing a library with a diverse range of structures .

While the subsequent description of the invention uses examples from the pharmaceutical industry, the present invention is not limited to the pharmaceutical industry. The present invention is equally adapted to classifying all types of chemical compounds which have ring structures .

In an alternate embodiment, the classification system uses a different method for finding the designated number of longest simple cycles LC in the undirected graph G [ V, E, δ] as shown by the flowchart of Fig. 9a. In step 905, the method initializes the list of longest simple cycles LC to null. In step 910, the method sets a desired simple cycle length DL to the cardinality of the set of edges E. After step 910, DL will equal the number of edges in the undirected graph -G[V, E, δ] .

In step 915, the method determines whether the list of longest simple cycles LC contains fewer cycles than the designated number of simple cycles. If the list of longest simple cycles contains fewer cycles than the designated number of simple cycles, control proceeds to step 920.
In step 920, the method determines whether the undirected graph G [V, E, δ] has a simple cycle with a length which is greater than or equal to DL. If the undirected graph G [V, E, δ] contains a simple cycle with a length which is greater than or equal to DL, control proceeds to step 925. In step 925, the method marks the simple cycle with a length which is greater than or equal to DL.

In step 930, the method determines whether the length of the marked simple cycle is greater than DL. If the length of the marked simple cycle is not greater than DL, control proceeds to step 935. In step 935, the method stores the marked simple cycle and its corresponding length in the list of longest simple cycles. In step 940, the method decrements
DL before control proceeds to step 915.

If the length of the marked simple cycle is greater than DL as determined in step 930, control proceeds to step 920 to determine whether the undirected graph G[V, E, δ] has another simple cycle with a length which is greater than or equal to DL .

If the undirected graph G [V, E, δ] does not contain an unmarked simple cycle with a length which is greater than or equal to DL as determined in step 920, control proceeds to step 940 where DL is decremented in preparation for a search for an incrementally smaller simple cycle.
If the list of longest simple cycles LC contains the designated number of longest simple cycles as determined in step 915, the method terminates.

In another alternate embodiment, the classification 20 system executes a more efficient method for finding the designated number of longest simple cycles in the undirected graph G [V, E, δ] as illustrated by the flowchart of Figs. 10a and 10b. As is known to persons of ordinary skill in the art and as indicated by "Computers and Intractability" by Michael Garey and David Johnson ("Garay"), the task of finding the longest simple cycle in an arbitrary undirected graph G [V, E, δ] is non-deterministic polynomial time complete (NP- complete) . However, the task of finding the longest simple cycle in an arbitrary undirected graph G [V, E, δ] may be performed in polynomial time for particular types of graphs. J V For example, researchers have designed a polynomial algorithm for finding the longest cycle in a particular type of directed graph called a tournament. See C. Morrow and S. Goodman, "An
Efficient Algori thm for Finding A Longest Cycle in a Tournament ". Similarly, the method described by the flowchart of Figs. 10a and 10b finds the designated number of longest cycles in polynomial time for an undirected graph G [ V, E, δ] when the undirected graph G[V, E, δ] is a planar graph and when all the finite regions of the planar undirected graph G [V, E, δ] are adjacent to the infinite region of the undirected graph G[V, E, δ] .

As is known to persons of ordinary skill in the art, a finite undirected graph G [V, E, δ] is planar if it can be drawn on a plane in such a way that no two of its edges intersect except, possibly, at vertices. See, e.g. Preparata. Further, a necessary and sufficient condition for a graph G [V,

E, δ] to be planar is that it contains no partial subgraphs of either the star graph or the utility graph. An undirected graph G ' [V , E > δ1] is called a subgraph of an undirected graph G[V, E, δ] if V is a subset of V and if E < (a subset of E) consists of all the edges in E joining vertices in V. If E' is a subset of all edges joining vertices in V then G' is called a partial subgraph of G.

As is known to persons of ordinary skill in the art, a region of a planar undirected graph G [V, E, δ] is a domain of the plane surrounded by edges of the planar undirected graph G[V, E, δ] such that any two points in it can be joined -by a line without crossing any edge. See e.g., Preparata. The edges which touch a region contain a simple cycle called the contour of the region. Two regions are said to be adjacent if the contours of the two regions have at least one edge in common. Further, since there is one and only one region which is infinite in a planar graph G [V, E, δ] by definition in the sense that the area determined by its contour is infinite, all other regions are finite.
Accordingly, Figs. 10a and 10b show the flowchart of an method for determining the designated number of longest simple cycles in polynomial time on an undirected graph G[V, E, δ] which is planar and where all of the finite regions are adjacent to the infinite region. Since this method executes in polynomial time, it enables the classification scheme to operate on libraries containing molecules and chemical compounds with larger numbers of atoms and bonds as long as the molecules and compounds have corresponding undirected graphs G[V, E, δ] which are planar and where all of the finite regions are adjacent to the infinite region.

In step 1004, the method initializes the set of the designated number of the longest simple cycles LC in G [V, E, δ] to the null set. The set LC will hold the result from execution of the method. In step 1005, the method determines the set of the shortest simple cycles SSC of each vertex of the graph G [ V, E, δ] in a manner as known to persons of ordinary skill in the art. See e.g., Preparata. In step 1010, the method determines a set of border edges BE comprising the edges of the shortest simple cycles SSC which are adjacent to the infinite region of the planar undirected graph G [ V, E, δ] .
In step 1015, the method computes the number of adjacent regions for the regions corresponding to each shortest simple cycle ssc in the set of shortest simple cycles SSC. In step
1020, the method sorts the simple cycles ssc in the set of shortest simple cycles SSC by the number of adjacent regions.

In step 1025, the method stores the shortest simple cycles ssc from the set of shortest simple cycles SSC having the smallest number of adjacent regions in a set SSC . In step 1030, the method determines the length of the shortest simple cycles ssc in the set of shortest simple cycles with the smallest number
of adjacent regions SSC . In step 1035, the method sorts the shortest simple cycles ssc in the list of shortest simple cycles SSC with the smallest number of adjacent regions SSC by their lengths .

In step 1036, the method defines a set of shortest simple cycle combinations CC which will hold catenations of the shortest simple cycles ssc from the set of shortest simple cycles SSC. The method initializes the first number of the set of shortest simple cycle combinations CC to a null entry.
Next, the method appends the set of the shortest simple cycles with the smallest number of adjacent regions SSC to the set of simple cycle combinations CC.

In step 1040, the method determines whether there are any shortest simple cycle combinations CC in the set of shortest simple cycle combinations CC and whether the set of longest simple cycles LC contains less than the designated number of longest simple cycles. If there are any shortest simple cycle combinations CC in the set CC and if the set of longest simple cycles LC contains less than the designated number of longest simple cycles, control proceeds to step 1045. In step 1045, the method selects the first shortest simple cycle combination cc from the set of shortest simple cycle combinations CC and removes it from the set .

In step 1055, the method forms a modified set of border edges BE ' by copying the set of border edges BE and removing the edges of the shortest simple cycles ssc of the selected shortest simple cycle combination cc . The classification system discussed above can be called a ring descriptor classification system because it classifies molecules according to a designated number of the longest simple cycles appearing within the molecules .

The present invention further includes a second classification system called an extended ring descriptor
classification system. The extended ring descriptor classification system has more categories than the ring descriptor classification system because the extended ring descriptor classification system includes more structural information.

The extended ring descriptor classification system identifies each of its categories by a sequence of tuples having a designated length. Each tuple contains two non- negative integers. The first non-negative integer in the tuple represents a length of a ring in the molecule. The second non-negative integer in the tuple represents the number of rings in the molecule having that length. The first tuple in the sequence represents the rings with the longest length in the molecule. Each successive tuple in the sequence represents successively shorter rings in the molecule. Thus, the extended ring descriptor classification system identifies the number of rings having particular lengths while the ring descriptor classification system merely identifies the presence or absence of rings having particular lengths.

persons of ordinary skill in the art. See, e.g., Donald Erwin Knuth, "The Art of Computer Programming" (3rd Edition) .

The ability of a classification system to distinguish complex rings from simple rings is important as structures containing rings with complex interconnections may correspond to chemical compounds which are not physically possible in the real world.

In an alternate embodiment, the resolution of the extended ring descriptor classification system is further increased by also identifying the types of atoms appearing within the rings. Specifically, this modified extended ring descriptor classification system attaches type attributes to the vertices representing atoms in the undirected graph G [V, E, δ] . The type attribute of a vertex identifies the type of the atom corresponding to the vertex such as carbon, silicon, and nitrogen.

In an alternate embodiment, the resolution of the extended ring descriptor classification system is further increased by also identifying the types of atoms appearing adjacent to the rings. Specifically, this modified extended ring descriptor classification system attaches neighboring type attributes to the vertices representing atoms in the undirected graph G [V, E, δ] . The neighboring type attribute of a vertex identifies the types of the atoms corresponding to neighboring vertices such as carbon, silicon, and nitrogen.
The extended ring descriptor classification system and its modifications provide higher resolution than the ring descriptor classification system. For example, there are a very large number of chemical compounds which fall into the same category 16, 15, 14, 13, 12, 11, 10, 9, 8, 7, 6, 5, 4, 3 of the ring descriptor classification system. The extended ring descriptor classification system distinguishes between the chemical compounds having the same ring descriptor by assigning them among different categories. As previously . . discussed these categories are defined by the number of rings having a particular length, the types of atoms within these rings and the types of atoms connected to these rings .

See Preparata. Next, the method records the degree for all vertices from V which are
reachable from vertex V by a path of length two. This process iterates until the method records the degree of all vertices from V which are reachable from vertex v' by a path with a predetermined maximum length.

The latter type of functions f (x) are well known to persons of ordinary skill in the art of cryptography and are used for creating fingerprints of documents.
